title: Applied anatomy: blood supply of the stomach and duodenum and the bleeding duodenal ulcer

related.why: Upper abdominal access and vessels at risk

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the surgical take
brief.scenario: Mr Graham Pike, 58, takes ibuprofen for back pain. He presented with melaena and haematemesis. Endoscopy showed a posterior duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel, treated with clips and adrenaline. Twelve hours later he has another haematemesis and is hypotensive. The examiner will ask you about the arterial anatomy of the stomach and duodenum, and will read out angiogram findings.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the blood supply of the stomach and duodenum, and relate them to his bleeding.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Coeliac trunk, stomach, duodenum, then why a posterior ulcer bleeds and what to do when it rebleeds.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Jumping to vagotomy or gastrectomy. For an unstable rebleed, think interventional radiology first.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The coeliac trunk gives left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries."

grid.label: Coeliac trunk
grid.pass: Arises from the aorta at T12; gives left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
grid.high: Adds that the common hepatic divides into the proper hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries, and that branching patterns vary.

grid.label: Stomach supply
grid.fail: Names fewer than the curvature arteries, or mixes up their origins.
grid.pass: Lesser curve: left gastric (coeliac) and right gastric (hepatic). Greater curve: left gastro-omental and short gastrics (splenic), right gastro-omental (gastroduodenal).
grid.high: Explains the rich anastomoses let the stomach survive division of several arteries, which is why a gastric conduit can rely on the right gastro-omental artery.

grid.label: Duodenal supply
grid.fail: Does not mention the pancreaticoduodenal arcade.
grid.pass: Gastroduodenal artery and its superior pancreaticoduodenal branches, anastomosing with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal from the superior mesenteric artery.
grid.high: Links the arcade to the foregut-midgut junction in the second part of the duodenum, and explains why embolising one side may not stop bleeding.

grid.label: Why a posterior ulcer bleeds
grid.fail: Cannot relate the ulcer to a named artery.
grid.pass: The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum; a posterior ulcer erodes into it.
grid.high: Adds that the artery is large and fed from both ends through the arcade, so bleeding can be torrential and recur.

grid.label: Managing the rebleed
grid.fail: Suggests waiting, or goes straight to gastrectomy.
grid.pass: Resuscitates and escalates. Unstable after endoscopic treatment: interventional radiology embolisation; urgent surgery if not promptly available (NICE CG141).
grid.high: Adds that a repeat endoscopy is offered to patients who rebleed, and involves the anaesthetist, radiologist and senior surgeon early.

grid.label: Surgical control
grid.fail: Proposes vagotomy and pyloroplasty as the standard operation, or cannot describe control.
grid.pass: Duodenotomy, under-running of the gastroduodenal artery with sutures above and below the ulcer.
grid.high: Adds a third suture for the transverse pancreatic branch and care to avoid the common bile duct; vagotomy is now historical.

grid.label: Aftercare
grid.fail: Restarts the NSAID or omits acid suppression.
grid.pass: Proton pump inhibitor after endoscopy with stigmata of recent haemorrhage; stops the NSAID.
grid.high: Adds Helicobacter pylori testing and treatment, and continuing low-dose aspirin if prescribed for secondary prevention once haemostasis is achieved.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Left gastric, splenic, common hepatic. The common hepatic divides into proper hepatic and gastroduodenal. The pattern varies, which matters to the radiologist.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why does the stomach tolerate ligation?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The arcades on both curves anastomose richly, so after oesophagectomy the gastric conduit can survive on the right gastro-omental artery.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The arcade links the foregut and midgut supply in the second part of the duodenum, so the bleeding point can fill from below.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The artery is large and fed from both ends, so bleeding can be torrential and recur.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: NICE also recommends repeat endoscopy for rebleeding, but he's unstable, so I'd involve the anaesthetist, radiologist and my consultant now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Above and below the ulcer, plus a third for the transverse pancreatic branch, keeping clear of the common bile duct. Vagotomy is now of historical interest.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Test and treat Helicobacter pylori. If he were on low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention, I'd continue it once haemostasis is achieved.

failures.move: Delaying escalation or going straight to gastrectomy.
failures.consequence: An unstable patient bleeds while a less invasive, faster option is missed.
Cannot explain the bleeding or target embolisation or suture.

failures.move: Offering vagotomy and pyloroplasty as standard.
failures.consequence: Adds morbidity without controlling the bleeding vessel.
Raises the risk of further bleeding.

recovery.when: You blank on the stomach supply
recovery.line: Two arteries on each curve plus the short gastrics: work back to coeliac branches.
If he's unstable after endoscopy, I'd ask for interventional radiology first, with surgery if it isn't promptly available.

knowledge.fact: Coeliac trunk at T12: left gastric, splenic, common hepatic.
Gastroduodenal artery lies behind the first part of the duodenum.
Superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries form an arcade.
Unstable rebleed after endoscopic treatment: interventional radiology; urgent surgery if not promptly available.
Surgical control: duodenotomy and under-running of the gastroduodenal artery.
Stop NSAIDs; proton pump inhibitor after endoscopy with stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

recall.think: Posterior duodenal ulcer rebleeding: gastroduodenal artery.
recall.say: "Unstable rebleed after endoscopy: interventional radiology, surgery if not promptly available."
do: Duodenotomy and under-run if surgery needed
recall.trap: Vagotomy and gastrectomy are not the default answer.
recall.finish: Embolisation or under-running; PPI, stop NSAID, test for Helicobacter pylori.

partner.opening: Mr Pike has rebled from his duodenal ulcer. Name the branches of the coeliac trunk.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations after the rebleed
Candidate asks whether interventional radiology is available
reveals.finding: The interventional radiologist can start in 30 minutes.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks what the angiogram shows
reveals.finding: Read out: a selective coeliac angiogram shows the trunk dividing into three branches. The branch running to the right divides into a vessel that ascends towards the liver and a vessel that descends behind the first part of the duodenum. The radiologist plans to embolise the descending vessel. What is it, and where does it come from?
Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily; no aspirin or anticoagulant.

push.question: What supplies the greater curvature?
push.expect: Short gastrics, left and right gastro-omental.

push.question: In a dissection of the stomach, an artery runs along the greater curvature from right to left, starting just below the pylorus, and meets another coming from the left. Name the two arteries and the vessel each arises from.
push.expect: Right gastro-omental from the gastroduodenal; left gastro-omental from the splenic.

push.question: In a diagram of the head of the pancreas, an arterial arcade lies in the curve of the duodenum, joining a branch coming from above with a branch coming from below. Which arteries form it, and why does it matter if the bleeding vessel is embolised?
push.expect: Superior pancreaticoduodenal (gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (superior mesenteric); the bleeding point can refill from below after embolisation.

push.question: Which artery bleeds in a posterior duodenal ulcer?
He is unstable after endoscopic treatment. What next?
push.expect: Interventional radiology; urgent surgery if not promptly available.

push.question: What would surgery involve?
push.expect: Duodenotomy and under-running the gastroduodenal artery.

curveballs.prompt: The radiologist is not available for four hours.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Refer urgently for surgery; continue resuscitation.

curveballs.prompt: Why not just do a vagotomy?
curveballs.safeAnswer: It does not control the bleeding vessel, and acid is now controlled with PPIs and Helicobacter eradication.

curveballs.prompt: The gastroduodenal artery is embolised but he bleeds again.
curveballs.safeAnswer: The arcade may fill it from the superior mesenteric side: discuss further embolisation or surgery with the team.
